…precedence—why reproach him for that? Yet disorder arises by using ceremonial observances and positions of precedence as its stepping-stones. Once Song made support or opposition the basis for assigning higher and lower rank, and no one corrected this, matters proceeded to Xu taking precedence over Xing and Qi over Song: relative strength determined who stood above or below whom. Again no one corrected this, until Chu contested precedence in sipping the sacrificial blood and Wu contested leadership, and the great safeguards collapsed. Had Duke Zhuang of Song led others according to ritual propriety, the feudal lords would have had no bad example to imitate. Even if laws and institutions had disappeared, distinctions of status would still have remained. However powerful Wu and Chu became, would they have dared? From the Spring and Autumn Annals’ record of the meeting at Cao and the attack on Zheng, the gentleman recognizes the far-reaching foresight of the Sage.

也此作得之
觀誠信之能感人而伯主貴戚之美見矣此晉
悼之誠以服鄭子鮮之信以喻喜皆春秋之僅
見者歟且夫伯駢行成蕭魚所為會也說者謂
晉悼之誠足以服人者何盖晉常争鄭以兵而
鄭不服至是子展盟而禮囚歸叔肹遣而侵掠
禁則推誠而不疑於鄭矣是故鄭自茲會惟晉
是與雖三駕之後甘楚之執而不敢晉悼之背
者非有所強也其誠有足懷耳不然反覆之國
===
===
尋盟尋叛其常也而何能久於晉耶噫大舜舞
干羽而苗格以其誠在令外也悼之於鄭不亦

其歸觀其營外取重於成叔言道見悅於臧孫

也，此作得之。
觀誠信之能感人，而伯主貴戚之美見矣。此晉悼之誠以服鄭、子鮮之信以喻喜，皆春秋之僅見者歟！且夫伯駢行成，蕭魚所為會也。說者謂晉悼之誠足以服人者何？盖晉常争鄭以兵，而鄭不服。至是，子展盟而禮囚歸，叔肹遣而侵掠禁，則推誠而不疑於鄭矣。是故鄭自茲會，惟晉是與。雖三駕之後，甘楚之執而不敢晉悼之背者，非有所強也，其誠有足懷耳。不然，反覆之國，尋盟尋叛，其常也，而何能久於晉耶？噫！大舜舞干羽而苗格，以其誠在令外也。悼之於鄭，不亦庶幾也哉！鱄喜約言，衛獻所由歸也。說者謂子鮮之信足以喻人者何？盖鱄嘗從獻以出，而圖其歸。觀其營外取重於成叔，言道見悅於臧孫，則以賢而素信於人矣。是故喜曰：「君歸必子鮮在。」雖千乘之君，不重其盟，而惟子鮮之重者，非有所私也，其信有足仗耳。不然，推輓之臣，或出或守，亦多矣，而何獨取於鱄耶？噫！小邾射恃季
translation_en:
…This essay has grasped it.
By observing how sincerity and trustworthiness can move others, we see the admirable qualities of a hegemon and a noble kinsman. Duke Dao of Jin’s sincerity in winning Zheng’s submission and Zixian’s trustworthiness in persuading Xi—were these not rare examples in the Spring and Autumn period? Now, Bo Pian’s negotiation of peace was the purpose of the meeting at Xiaoyu. Why do commentators say that Duke Dao of Jin’s sincerity was sufficient to win others’ submission? Jin had repeatedly contended for Zheng by force of arms, yet Zheng would not submit. On this occasion, however, Zizhan swore the covenant, the prisoners were treated courteously and returned, Shu Xi was sent back, and incursions and plundering were forbidden. Thus Jin dealt sincerely with Zheng, without suspicion. Consequently, from this meeting onward, Zheng allied itself exclusively with Jin. After the three campaigns, it willingly endured detention by Chu rather than dare turn its back on Duke Dao of Jin. This was not because it was compelled: his sincerity was sufficient to win its allegiance. Otherwise, a fickle state habitually breaks a covenant almost as soon as it concludes one; how could Zheng have remained loyal to Jin for so long? Ah! The great Shun performed the dance with shields and feathers, and the Miao submitted, because his sincerity worked beyond the reach of commands. Did not Duke Dao’s dealings with Zheng come close to this?
The agreement between Zhuan and Xi was what enabled Duke Xian of Wei to return. Why do commentators say that Zixian’s trustworthiness was sufficient to persuade others? Zhuan had accompanied Duke Xian into exile and planned his return. Consider how, through his efforts abroad, he won Chengshu’s esteem, and how his discussion of the Way pleased Zangsun: his worthiness had long earned others’ trust. Thus Xi said, “If the ruler returns, Zixian must be present.” Although the ruler commanded a thousand chariots, Xi placed no weight on his sworn pledge, valuing only Zixian’s assurance. This was not a matter of personal partiality: Zixian’s trustworthiness offered something on which he could rely. Otherwise, there were many ministers working to advance the ruler’s cause, some accompanying him into exile and others remaining at home; why choose Zhuan alone? Ah! Yi of Xiaozhu relied on Ji…

translation_en:
…[illegible] and did not enter into a covenant, because his trustworthiness preceded his words. Can Zhuan’s position in Wei not be spoken of in the same terms? Thus, when we observe how Duke Dao brought Zheng into submission without issuing commands, we understand that sincerity must never cease; when we observe how Zhuan reassured Xi without speaking, we understand that trustworthiness must never cease. Duke Jing of Jin provoked divided loyalties among the feudal lords. Instead of attending to sincerity and trustworthiness, he sought to bind them through the covenant at Pu. The Spring and Autumn Annals had good reason to censure him!

Even so, Duke Dao succeeded in pacifying Zheng but failed in winning over Chen; Zhuan bound Xi by an agreement at the outset but could not protect him in the end. Why was this? Xi’s encounter with disaster resulted from Mianyu’s conduct [?]; the entrusting of his son at Mumen was indeed poignant. Yet “Having Chen is no concern of ours” was merely a statement by Shi Gai alone. Did Zhi Ying and the other ministers not participate in the undertaking to garrison Chen? Thus, governing a state rests fundamentally on obtaining worthy men, and encouraging worthy men requires, first of all, eliminating slander.

text:
考試官大學士袁批文整而意盡
記者即樂之聲與體而擬諸天地焉夫清明廣
大至于天地極矣而樂之聲與體象之此其所
以為妙也歟且夫正樂之作人知其用之大也
然不觀其法制之詳抑何以見其感通之本哉
何則樂必有聲而聲之清明則象天焉夫穹焉
窿焉超形器而獨存者天也樂之聲何以擬之
盖清明者天以之運其氣樂亦以之播其聲其
究一而已矣八音之和動瑩然無所雜者即其
===
輕清上浮而不可踰也六律之昭宣曒然無所
紊者即其光明下濟而不容掩也是聲雖不可
以同天而語其清明之極則非天無以為之象

化之神範圍而不過者猶夫厚德載物莫能窮
其至也備倫理之衆兼統而無遺者猶夫坤順

The author of the Record takes the sound and embodied form of music and compares them to Heaven and Earth. Clarity and brightness, breadth and greatness, reach their utmost in Heaven and Earth; the sound and form of music imitate them. Is this not what makes music wondrous? People know the greatness of the function served by the creation of orthodox music. Yet without examining the details of its rules and institutions, how can they discern the foundation of its power to evoke response and establish communion? Why is this so? Music necessarily has sound, and the clarity and brightness of its sound imitate Heaven. Vaulted and lofty, existing independently beyond material forms and vessels: such is Heaven. How can the sound of music be compared to it? Through clarity and brightness, Heaven circulates its vital force; through these same qualities, music propagates its sound. In their ultimate principle, they are one. The harmonious stirring of the eight classes of musical instruments, pure and unmixed, is precisely like Heaven’s light and clear vital force floating upward, beyond which nothing can rise. The radiant expression of the six pitch standards, bright and undisturbed, is precisely like Heaven’s light reaching downward, admitting no concealment. Although this sound cannot be equated with Heaven, when we speak of its utmost clarity and brightness, nothing but Heaven can serve as its likeness. Is not such sound, which imitates Heaven, the excellence of sound?

Music necessarily has an embodied form, and the breadth and greatness of that form imitate Earth. Broad and thick, matching Heaven’s virtue and without bounds: such is Earth. How can the form of music be compared to it? Through breadth and greatness, Earth achieves its shape; through these same qualities, music establishes its form. The measure governing them is one. Music encompasses the spiritual efficacy of shared transformation, embracing it without exceeding its bounds, just as Earth, through its ample virtue, bears all things, and none can exhaust its reach. Music includes the manifold ordered relationships, comprehending them all without omission, just as the yielding receptivity of Kun, Earth …

translation_en:
…bring this out.

The sage makes manifest the transforming influence of the noble man's rites and music, and accordingly explains its workings in detail. That people and things follow their proper courses marks the flourishing of government and moral transformation. Yet unless one seeks rites and music within oneself, how could one bring this about? When the Master formerly answered Zizhang's question about government, his discussion reached this point. His meaning was that the Way of rites and music lies within oneself, but, when extended, embraces all under Heaven. It is precisely because the noble man understands this that he devotes himself to it. Thus his upright and balanced conduct deepens the trust inspired by his dignified bearing. A model is established, and those who behold it share in its transforming influence; orderly and tranquil government thereby spreads everywhere. His harmonious and peaceful music conveys the beauty of joyful movement. Gladness circulates and harmonious vital energies flow freely; universal concord naturally results. Perfect order and perfect harmony fill the space between Heaven and Earth, while comprehensive accord and transformation converge upon the sovereign's supreme standard. All under Heaven is thereby brought to peace.

Thus, although the feudal lords govern separate parts of the realm and their circumstances are exceedingly dispersed, they emulate my virtue of harmony and order and together demonstrate their sincere support and allegiance. They come to present offerings and pay court, united in virtue in honoring the Son of Heaven: their territories differ, but their hearts do not. Could any fail to submit? The myriad things appear scattered throughout the world, and their incipient workings are exceedingly complex. Yet they follow my guiding principles of harmony and order and all accord with the measure of rectitude. Proceeding together and proceeding in detail [?], adapting to change so as to realize their full benefits, they have no fixed forms but do have constant principles. Could any fail to conform to their proper constitution? Likewise, the officials arrayed at court, who assist in governing all under Heaven, occupy unequal ranks. Yet they look up to virtue and receive its blessings, allowing themselves no respite in fulfilling their duties, each according to his allotted responsibility establishing…

translation_en:
…loyalty, and strive in their service for fear of falling behind. All follow due order and are harmonious at heart, assisting their sovereign. Who, then, would dare relax the sincerity with which he serves? This is what is called the flourishing of Great Peace, the highest achievement of government. If we trace its source, it all comes back to the Way of rites and music. Thus it is said: “Once the gentleman understands rites and music, he need only put them into practice.” Shi [Zizhang], what further perplexity have you?
Yet Confucius once answered Master Yan’s question about governing a state by referring to the rites and music of the four dynasties. Why, here, does he speak of rites and music solely in terms of harmony and order within oneself? Master Yan already possessed the virtues of harmony and order, whereas Zizhang pursued external things and aimed excessively high. The Master therefore taught him to turn back to himself and seek them there. Devoting effort to oneself is the foundation of rites and music; weighing the institutions of the former kings and putting them into use supplies their outward forms. With both foundation and outward forms present, the Kingly Way is complete. Students should consider the two together.

The Ruler’s Exalted Status Is Like That of Heaven
Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Examining Editor: Serving one’s ruler as one serves Heaven is the rule for subjects throughout all ages. Wang Xijue

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
同考試官侍讀汪批君尊如天士子類言之未得
肯綮此作歸於臣任其勞而君之尊乃顯深為有見
且體裁高古議論雅馴而開闔抑揚卓有奇氣必
忠愛之誠素蓄於衷者取冠多士匪直以其文已也
考試官學士董批古人作論本借題以發明大
意未嘗小拘也子能于和靖言表究極其指以明
君臣之分非忠義蓄積于中何以有此取冠多士宜矣
考試官大學士袁批握域中之大權曰天曰君天運
於上而不勞君之尊與天並者以此吾子獨得其意
===
而詞義高古足以發之必能以天事
君矣首薦允宜
人君之尊天所命也人臣之尊其君亦天所命
也人君法天以治天下故能獨成其尊人臣事
君如事天故其君之尊益至法天者端拱于上
者也事君如事天者盡職于下者也端拱于上
是以運天下而不勞盡職于下是以任勞而不
敢懈運而不勞以得其臣也得其臣則治成治
成則君逸而天下益仰其尊勞而不敢懈以體

人君之尊，天所命也；人臣之尊其君，亦天所命也。人君法天以治天下，故能獨成其尊；人臣事君如事天，故其君之尊益至。法天者，端拱于上者也；事君如事天者，盡職于下者也。端拱于上，是以運天下而不勞；盡職于下，是以任勞而不敢懈。運而不勞，以得其臣也。得其臣則治成，治成則君逸，而天下益仰其尊。勞而不敢懈，以體

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Reader-in-waiting: Candidates commonly say that the ruler is as exalted as Heaven, but they fail to grasp the essential point. This essay locates it in the minister’s undertaking the toil, through which the ruler’s exalted status becomes manifest—a profound insight. Moreover, its form is lofty and antique, its argument refined and well ordered, and its development and shifts of emphasis display an extraordinary vigor. Its author must long have cherished sincere loyalty and devotion in his heart. In placing him first among the candidates, we value more than his writing alone.

Comment by Examiner Dong, Academician: When the ancients composed discourses, they used the topic to elucidate a larger meaning and never confined themselves to petty details. You have gone beyond Hejing’s words to fathom their ultimate purport and clarify the respective duties of ruler and minister. Without loyalty and righteousness accumulated within, how could you have achieved this? It is fitting to place you first among the candidates.

Comment by Examiner Yuan, Grand Secretary: Those who wield supreme authority within the realm are Heaven and the ruler. Heaven moves above without toil; it is in this respect that the ruler’s exalted status equals Heaven’s. You alone have grasped this meaning, and the lofty, antique quality of your language and ideas suffices to express it. You will surely be able to serve the ruler as you would Heaven. Recommending you first is entirely fitting.

The ruler’s exalted status is ordained by Heaven; the minister’s reverence for his ruler is likewise ordained by Heaven. The ruler models himself on Heaven in governing all under Heaven and thus alone attains this exalted status. Ministers serve their ruler as they serve Heaven, and thus their ruler’s exalted status becomes still greater. To model oneself on Heaven is to sit upright above with hands folded; to serve the ruler as one serves Heaven is to fulfill one’s duties below. That the ruler directs affairs without toil is because he has obtained the right ministers. With the right ministers, good government is achieved; with good government achieved, the ruler enjoys repose, and all under Heaven look up to his exalted status still more. That ministers toil and dare not slacken is because they consider…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
其君也體其君則政事理政事理則君無為而
益顯其尊于天下此君之尊所以上與天並而
實君臣之大分天下之至理非有所強焉者也
宋儒尹氏知道者也曰人君其尊如天言人臣
當知所尊也明臣道也而吾本人君之所以為
尊者言之明君道也斯二者蓋互相發也吾嘗
觀諸天矣今夫天下之人孰不知天之尊者古
今孰不能言天之尊者而欲求其所以為尊則
未易見也將以其巍然峻極者言之歟斯以形
===
言天矣未得其所以為尊也將以其造育天下
者言之歟斯以用言天矣未盡其所以為尊也
夫五行之序四時之紀日月之照雨露之濡風
雷之鼓震此五者天之所以為造育者也使天
而無以運之則五者或失其統而天之化機窒
矣何以為尊也使五者不得其職而必待于天
自為之則天不勝其勞而其化機紊矣又何以
為尊也天惟密運于上而序之為五行紀之為
四時照臨之以日月沾濡之以雨露鼓動震盪

其君也體其君則致事理致事理則君無爲而
益顯其尊于天下此君之尊所以上與天並而
實君臣之大分天下之至理非有所强焉者也
宋儒尹氏知道者也曰人君其尊如天言人臣

今孰不能言天之尊者而欲求其所以爲尊則
未易見也將以其巍然峻極者言之歟斯以形
===
言天矣未得其所以爲尊也將以其造育天下
者言之歟斯以用言天矣未盡其所以爲尊也
夫五行之序四時之紀日月之照雨露之濡風

而無以運之則五者或失其統而天之化機窒
矣何以爲尊也使五者不得其職而必待于天
自爲之則天不勝其勞而其化機紊矣又何以
爲尊也天惟密運于上而序之爲五行紀之爲
四時照臨之以日月沾濡之以雨露鼓動震盪
punctuated:
其君也。體其君則政事理，政事理則君無為而益顯其尊于天下。此君之尊所以上與天並，而實君臣之大分、天下之至理，非有所強焉者也。宋儒尹氏，知道者也，曰：「人君其尊如天。」言人臣當知所尊也，明臣道也。而吾本人君之所以為尊者言之，明君道也。斯二者蓋互相發也。
吾嘗觀諸天矣。今夫天下之人，孰不知天之尊者？古今孰不能言天之尊者？而欲求其所以為尊，則未易見也。將以其巍然峻極者言之歟？斯以形言天矣，未得其所以為尊也。將以其造育天下者言之歟？斯以用言天矣，未盡其所以為尊也。夫五行之序、四時之紀、日月之照、雨露之濡、風雷之鼓震，此五者，天之所以為造育者也。使天而無以運之，則五者或失其統，而天之化機窒矣，何以為尊也？使五者不得其職，而必待于天自為之，則天不勝其勞，而其化機紊矣，又何以為尊也？天惟密運于上，而序之為五行，紀之為四時，照臨之以日月，沾濡之以雨露，鼓動震盪
translation_en:
…their ruler. When ministers take their ruler’s concerns to heart, affairs of government are well ordered; when affairs of government are well ordered, the ruler acts without exertion, and his exalted standing becomes still more manifest throughout the realm. This is why the ruler’s exalted standing ranks alongside Heaven’s. It is indeed the great distinction between ruler and minister and the supreme principle of the world, with nothing forced about it. Master Yin, the Song Confucian scholar, understood the Way. He said: “The ruler is as exalted as Heaven.” This means that ministers should know whom to revere, and elucidates the Way of the minister. I, however, speak from the basis of what makes the ruler exalted, elucidating the Way of the ruler. These two explanations illuminate one another.
I have sought to understand this by observing Heaven. Among all people in the world, who does not know that Heaven is exalted? From antiquity to the present, who has been unable to speak of Heaven’s exalted standing? Yet if we seek what makes it exalted, this is not readily discerned. Shall we speak of its towering height? That describes Heaven in terms of its form, without grasping what makes it exalted. Shall we speak of its creation and nurture of all beneath it? That describes Heaven in terms of its operation, without fully explaining what makes it exalted. The ordered succession of the Five Phases, the regular course of the four seasons, the illumination of sun and moon, the moistening of rain and dew, and the stirring and shaking of wind and thunder—these five are the means by which Heaven creates and nurtures. If Heaven had no means of setting them in motion, these five might lose their governing order, and Heaven’s workings of transformation would be obstructed. How, then, could it be exalted? If these five could not fulfill their respective offices, but had to wait for Heaven itself to perform them, Heaven could not bear the toil, and its workings of transformation would fall into disorder. How, again, could it be exalted? Heaven simply operates unseen above: it establishes order through the Five Phases, regulates the course of time through the four seasons, shines down with sun and moon, moistens with rain and dew, and stirs and shakes…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
之以風雷周流循環而不可窮倏忽變化而不
可測萬物以生以成而不知其所使以為非天
耶而主宰之者何也以為天耶而天則何為也
孰根柢是而特不得其故孰推行是而特不得
其端於穆深遠而後知為天之尊也嗟乎此君
道也帝王之盡君道者莫如堯舜孔子稱惟天
為大惟堯則之君哉舜也恭已正南面而已矣
後世而下可以想見其尊而覽觀載記堯舜之
時亦多故矣其大者洪水横流有苗弗率而當
===
其時寇賊奸宄未除禮樂未制五教未明天下
之州牧尚未得其理宜二帝之不暇給而所以
能成其尊者何也則以君道運于上而臣職盡
于下也故洪水則禹治之有苗則禹征之未嘗
以勞二帝也寇賊奸宄則臯陶掌之未嘗以勞
二帝也禮樂則夔夷典之未嘗以勞二帝也五
教則契敷之未嘗以勞二帝也九州十二牧則
四岳統之未嘗以勞二帝也當時之臣不以勞
其君而皆各任其職是能尊其君者也是□

之以風雷，周流循環而不可窮，倏忽變化而不可測。萬物以生以成，而不知其所使。以為非天耶，而主宰之者何也？以為天耶，而天則何為也？孰根柢是，而特不得其故？孰推行是，而特不得其端？於穆深遠，而後知為天之尊也。
嗟乎！此君道也。帝王之盡君道者，莫如堯舜。孔子稱：「惟天為大，惟堯則之。」「君哉舜也！」「恭已正南面而已矣。」後世而下，可以想見其尊。而覽觀載記，堯舜之時亦多故矣。其大者，洪水横流，有苗弗率。而當其時，寇賊奸宄未除，禮樂未制，五教未明，天下之州牧尚未得其理。宜二帝之不暇給，而所以能成其尊者何也？則以君道運于上，而臣職盡于下也。故洪水則禹治之，有苗則禹征之，未嘗以勞二帝也；寇賊奸宄則臯陶掌之，未嘗以勞二帝也；禮樂則夔夷典之，未嘗以勞二帝也；五教則契敷之，未嘗以勞二帝也；九州十二牧則四岳統之，未嘗以勞二帝也。當時之臣不以勞其君，而皆各任其職，是能尊其君者也。是□
translation_en:
…them with wind and thunder, circulating in unending cycles and changing with a swiftness beyond fathoming. The myriad things are thus born and brought to completion, yet do not know what makes them so. If one holds that it is not Heaven, what governs them? If one holds that it is Heaven, what does Heaven itself do? Who gives all this its foundation? Yet its underlying cause cannot be discovered. Who sets all this in motion? Yet its origin cannot be found. August, profound, and far-reaching—only then does one understand Heaven’s exalted standing.
Alas! This is the Way of the ruler. Among emperors and kings, none fulfilled the Way of the ruler as fully as Yao and Shun. Confucius declared: “Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone modeled himself upon it”; “What a ruler Shun was!”; and “He merely held himself reverently and took his proper place facing south.” Later generations can thus imagine their exalted standing. Yet when we examine the records, the age of Yao and Shun also had many troubles. The greatest were the floodwaters overflowing their bounds and the refusal of the Youmiao to submit. At that time, robbers, thieves, and evildoers within and without had not been eliminated; rites and music had not been established; the five teachings had not been made clear; and the regional governors throughout the realm had not yet achieved orderly government. One would expect the two emperors to have been overwhelmed. How, then, could they attain their exalted standing? It was because the Way of the ruler operated above, while ministers fully discharged their duties below. Thus Yu controlled the floodwaters, and Yu campaigned against the Youmiao, without ever burdening the two emperors. Gao Yao dealt with robbers, thieves, and evildoers within and without, without ever burdening the two emperors. Kui and Yi took charge of rites and music, without ever burdening the two emperors. Xie spread the five teachings, without ever burdening the two emperors. The Four Peaks oversaw the Nine Regions and the twelve regional governors, without ever burdening the two emperors. The ministers of that time did not burden their ruler; each undertook his own duties. These were men who could uphold their ruler’s exalted standing. These [illegible; ?]…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
事君如天者也而二帝于其時但見其地平天
成而已矣但見其舞干振羽而已矣而上無勞
焉又但見其四方從欲而已矣而上無勞焉又
但見其鬼神咸格鳳凰來儀而已矣而上無勞
焉又但見其五品以遜百姓以治萬邦咸寧而
已矣而上無勞焉運而不勞猶天之運也不勞
而成化猶天之于造育也故天下後世知天之
尊則知二帝之尊言二帝之尊者必比于天之
尊歷億千萬年而不改者非有所強也嗟乎此
===
君道也故人君者履大寶握中樞位曰天位而
天下之位莫加焉天所命也膺歷數纘帝極統
曰天統而天下之統莫加焉天所命也合天下
邦國之奉祿曰天祿而天下之祿莫加焉天所
命也人臣者受位與祿于君而賛君以承天之
統者也亦天所命也天將付人君以撫御四海
之權裁成萬物之道而代其造育之功則命之
不得以不尊天將使人君以獨成其尊則不得
不列百執事之臣以各任其職故君者天所命

punctuated:
事君如天者也。而二帝于其時，但見其地平天成而已矣，但見其舞干振羽而已矣，而上無勞焉；又但見其四方從欲而已矣，而上無勞焉；又但見其鬼神咸格、鳳凰來儀而已矣，而上無勞焉；又但見其五品以遜、百姓以治、萬邦咸寧而已矣，而上無勞焉。運而不勞，猶天之運也；不勞而成化，猶天之于造育也。故天下後世知天之尊，則知二帝之尊；言二帝之尊者，必比于天之尊，歷億千萬年而不改者，非有所強也。嗟乎！此君道也。
故人君者，履大寶，握中樞，位曰天位，而天下之位莫加焉，天所命也；膺歷數，纘帝極，統曰天統，而天下之統莫加焉，天所命也；合天下邦國之奉，祿曰天祿，而天下之祿莫加焉，天所命也。人臣者，受位與祿于君，而賛君以承天之統者也，亦天所命也。天將付人君以撫御四海之權、裁成萬物之道，而代其造育之功，則命之不得以不尊。天將使人君以獨成其尊，則不得不列百執事之臣，以各任其職。故君者，天所命
translation_en:
…those who serve their ruler as they would Heaven. In their time, the Two Emperors merely saw the earth brought to order and Heaven’s work accomplished; they merely saw the dances with shields and waving plumes, while they themselves, above, underwent no toil. They merely saw the four quarters conform to their wishes, while they themselves underwent no toil. They merely saw the spirits all arrive and the phoenixes come in stately array, while they themselves underwent no toil. They merely saw the five human relationships observed harmoniously, the people well governed, and the myriad states all at peace, while they themselves underwent no toil. To set things in motion without toil is like Heaven’s movement; to bring about transformation without toil is like Heaven’s creation and nurture. Thus, when the world and later generations recognize Heaven’s exalted standing, they recognize that of the Two Emperors. Those who speak of the Two Emperors’ exalted standing invariably compare it to Heaven’s. That this remains unchanged through countless millions of years is not the result of compulsion. Ah! This is the Way of the ruler.
Thus the ruler occupies the great throne and holds the central pivot of government. His position is called Heaven’s position, and no position under Heaven stands above it: this is Heaven’s mandate. He receives the allotted succession and continues the imperial sovereignty. His line of succession is called Heaven’s succession, and no succession under Heaven stands above it: this is Heaven’s mandate. He gathers the contributions of all the states under Heaven. His emoluments are called Heaven’s emoluments, and no emoluments under Heaven exceed them: this is Heaven’s mandate. Ministers receive their positions and emoluments from the ruler and assist him in carrying on Heaven’s succession: this too is Heaven’s mandate. Since Heaven would entrust the ruler with authority to nurture and govern all within the four seas, and with the Way of ordering and perfecting the myriad things, so that he may perform its work of creation and nurture in its stead, its mandate necessarily makes him exalted. Since Heaven would have the ruler alone attain this exalted standing, it must establish the ministers of the hundred offices, each to discharge his own duties. Thus the ruler is one whom Heaven has mandated…

Thus the ruler is the one whose regulations are followed, not one who follows another’s regulations [?]; the one who is served, not one who serves another; the one who is taken as a model, not one who takes another as his model. Should there be aggression by the Man and Yi peoples, this calls for the execution of Heaven’s punitive judgment and must not be neglected: the generals and commanders assume responsibility for it. title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
臣皆竭精盡思惟恐遺其君以勞所以亮天工
也人君坐而受成運而不勞所以體天道也體
天道者君之本尊也亮天工者人臣之所以成
其尊也故天下見其禮樂教化之行而不見其
勞曰是何文治之神也見其政刑之當不軌之
潜息強夷巨寇之咸頓而不見其勞曰是何武
治之神也見其方國之乂安捍災禦患之有道
而不見其勞曰是何加意于民而拊循之治之
神也若有以治之而亦不得其端若有以致之
===
而亦不得其故至此而人君之尊果與天並不
可得而測也其明也日月之照天之明也其恩
也雨露之濡天之恩也其威也風雷之鼓震天
之威也其政事之順布五行四時之循環天之
順也施之中國而愛戴施之八荒海外而歸服
施之昆蟲草木而得所施之舟車所至人力所
通凡有血氣而莫不知所尊故曰人君之尊如
天能與天運者也
表

施之昆蟲草木而得所施之舟車所至人力所
通凡有血氣而莫不知所尊故曰人君之尊如
天能與天運者也
表
punctuated:
臣皆竭精盡思，惟恐遺其君以勞，所以亮天工也。人君坐而受成，運而不勞，所以體天道也。體天道者，君之本尊也；亮天工者，人臣之所以成其尊也。故天下見其禮樂教化之行，而不見其勞，曰：「是何文治之神也！」見其政刑之當、不軌之潜息、強夷巨寇之咸頓，而不見其勞，曰：「是何武治之神也！」見其方國之乂安、捍災禦患之有道，而不見其勞，曰：「是何加意于民而拊循之治之神也！」若有以治之，而亦不得其端；若有以致之，而亦不得其故。至此而人君之尊，果與天並，不可得而測也。其明也，日月之照，天之明也；其恩也，雨露之濡，天之恩也；其威也，風雷之鼓震，天之威也；其政事之順布，五行四時之循環，天之順也。施之中國而愛戴，施之八荒海外而歸服，施之昆蟲草木而得所，施之舟車所至、人力所通，凡有血氣而莫不知所尊。故曰：「人君之尊如天，能與天運者也。」

表
translation_en:
…ministers all devote their utmost energy and thought, fearing only that they might leave their ruler with work to do: this is how they assist in Heaven’s work. The ruler sits and receives the accomplished results, setting things in motion without toil: this is how he embodies Heaven’s Way. Embodying Heaven’s Way is the foundation of the ruler’s exalted standing; assisting in Heaven’s work is how his ministers bring that standing to fulfillment. Thus, when all under Heaven see rites, music, instruction, and moral transformation put into practice, yet see no toil on his part, they say, “How wondrous is his civil governance!” When they see administration and punishments properly applied, wrongdoing quietly subsiding, and powerful foreign peoples and mighty bands of rebels all subdued, yet see no toil on his part, they say, “How wondrous is his military governance!” When they see the regions and states peacefully governed, and disasters warded off and calamities prevented by proper means, yet see no toil on his part, they say, “How wondrous is this governance that takes special care for the people and cherishes them!” It seems that there is something by which he governs them, yet its source cannot be discerned; it seems that there is something by which he brings these results about, yet its cause cannot be discerned. At this point, the ruler’s exalted standing truly equals Heaven’s and cannot be fathomed. His illumination is the shining of sun and moon—Heaven’s illumination. His beneficence is the moistening of rain and dew—Heaven’s beneficence. His might is the stirring and shaking of wind and thunder—Heaven’s might. The orderly unfolding of his administration is the cycle of the Five Phases and four seasons—Heaven’s order. Exercised in the Central States, his rule wins love and reverence; extended to the eight distant regions and lands beyond the seas, it wins allegiance and submission; extended to insects, grasses, and trees, it gives each its proper place. Wherever boats and carriages reach and human effort can penetrate, all beings possessing blood and breath know whom to revere. Thus it is said: “The ruler’s exalted standing is like Heaven’s: he can move in accord with Heaven.”

同考試官署郎中許批：才思淵博，詞藻典麗。我成祖昭格靈貺，闡揚極盡。子其名世之瑞乎？錄之。

同考試官檢討陸批：稱頌有體，鋪敘有倫，且典則流麗，而藻思充溢。我朝瑞應之盛，子其善於揄揚矣。可佳，可佳！

同考試官編修姚批：天錫仁獸，用昭我皇祖好生大德。子能頌揚盛美，而詞復雅麗，三復起敬。

同考試官右諭德唐批：我成祖至仁格天，竒祥昭應，未易形容也。是作能於四六中揚厲閎休，讀之宛若親見者，信可以彰盛美而垂無窮矣。錄之，不獨以文之工也。

translation_en:
Model memorial of congratulation from the assembled officials on the Prince of Zhou’s obtaining a zouyu, an auspicious beast, at Shenhou Mountain and presenting it to the throne. Second year of Yongle (1404). By Duan Mengxian.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Bureau Director: Your talent and thought are profound and extensive; your diction is classically refined and elegant. You have expounded to the fullest how our Chengzu’s luminous virtue called forth this divine blessing. Might you yourself be an auspicious talent destined for renown in this age? Include this piece.

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Examining Editor: The praise is fitting in form, and the exposition orderly. Moreover, the writing observes classical standards while flowing gracefully, and imaginative eloquence abounds. You are indeed skilled at celebrating the profusion of auspicious responses granted to our dynasty. Admirable, admirable!

Comment by Associate Examiner Yao, Compiler: Heaven bestowed this benevolent beast to manifest our imperial ancestor’s great virtue in cherishing life. You have succeeded in celebrating this splendid excellence, and your language is also refined and elegant. Repeated readings inspire reverence.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Right Exhorter of Virtue: Our Chengzu’s consummate benevolence reached Heaven, and extraordinary auspicious signs appeared in clear response. This is no easy thing to portray. This composition extols that vast glory in four- and six-character parallel prose. Reading it, one feels as though one had witnessed the event in person. It can assuredly make that splendid excellence manifest and transmit it for all time. Include it, and not merely for its literary craftsmanship.

昊天無疆之眷非特一時之慶也此作博雅典麗足以發之可式矣

成祖功德巍煥昭格
皇天玆神物呈瑞實兆億萬年太平之治子能表章靈貺而詞復純

天心篤佑竒祥祗薦於中州丕凝二極之和懋

昊天無疆之眷，非特一時之慶也。此作博雅典麗，足以發之，可式矣。
考試官大學士泰批：我成祖功德巍煥，昭格皇天。玆神物呈瑞，實兆億萬年太平之治。子能表章靈貺，而詞復純美，宜錄以傳。
永樂二年五月，周王得騶虞於鈞州神后山，以獻于朝。臣等誠懽誠忭，稽首頓首稱賀者。伏以帝德好生，協氣旁流於率土；天心篤佑，竒祥祗薦於中州。丕凝二極之和，懋迓三靈之祉。玄樞煥彩，聖世呈珍。竊惟君人位天地之中，則天祥降、地符出；王者爲民物之主，則民心順、物化彰。盖仁恩徧覆以無遺，斯志意交孚而罔間。淵機黙契，景貺昭垂。逖考前聞，咸有徵於鴻烈；歷稽上瑞，尤莫過於騶虞。稟金行，得純如之素質；精分水德，粲蔚矣之緇文。
translation_en:
…the boundless favor of August Heaven, rather than merely a cause for celebration on one occasion. This composition, erudite, refined, dignified, and elegant, adequately brings this out and may serve as a model.
Examiner and Grand Secretary Tai comments: Our Chengzu’s achievements and virtue were lofty and brilliant, reaching August Heaven. This divine creature’s appearance as an auspicious sign truly presaged peaceful government for countless millions of years. You have elucidated this numinous gift, and your language is also pure and beautiful. The piece deserves to be recorded and transmitted.
In the fifth month of the second year of Yongle [1404], the Prince of Zhou obtained a zouyu, an auspicious beast, at Mount Shenhou in Junzhou and presented it at court. We, your servants, in sincere delight and joy, bow our heads to the ground and knock our foreheads in congratulation. We humbly consider:
The Emperor’s virtue cherishes life, and harmonious vital energy spreads throughout all the land; Heaven’s will grants generous protection, and wondrous auspicious signs are reverently presented in the Central Region. Grandly is the harmony of the two poles, Heaven and Earth, brought together; earnestly are the blessings of the three numinous powers welcomed. The celestial pivot shines with radiance; a treasure appears in this sagely age. We humbly reflect that when the ruler of men takes his place between Heaven and Earth, auspicious signs descend from Heaven and tokens emerge from Earth; when the king acts as lord of the people and all creatures, the people’s hearts submit and the transformation of living things becomes manifest. For when benevolence and gracious favor encompass everything without omission, intentions respond to one another in mutual trust without estrangement. The profound workings silently accord, and glorious gifts visibly descend. Searching far back through accounts of antiquity, we find that all bear witness to magnificent achievements; examining the highest auspicious signs in succession, we find none surpassing the zouyu. Endowed with the phase of Metal, it possesses a pristine white substance; sharing in the essence of Water’s potency, it displays brilliantly patterned black markings…

text:
斂威揚愷悌之風覿德麗雍熙之治是盖
神物肇見堯時雲感高丘誕元精而佐舜
颸馳遠道懷明聖以歸湯逮於周室之興
遂入詩人之詠咀華行葦本忠厚於西岐
毓粹園林現休禎於南國洊更三季僅爾

體睿含靈
執中布度

對時茂育躋世和平萃諸福以駢臻合四靈
而畢至肆
璇穹錫眷益隆單厚之釐乃玉瑞涵姿正躡
明昌之會産從神后匪同豹隱於深山獻自
宗藩迥邁獒來於異域炳若大人之變象應
河圖睦然君子之能名標漢賦率兹百獸

斂威，揚愷悌之風；覿德，麗雍熙之治。是盖神物肇見堯時，雲感高丘，誕元精而佐舜；颸馳遠道，懷明聖以歸湯。逮於周室之興，遂入詩人之詠。咀華行葦，本忠厚於西岐；毓粹園林，現休禎於南國。洊更三季，僅爾傳聲；凡閱千年，復兹顯象。
恭惟皇帝陛下，體睿含靈，執中布度。赤光虎變，昭元命之貞符；紫極龍飛，協重華之盛際。萬國運於掌上，由推不忍之心；四夷在於目中，爰擴有容之量。對時茂育，躋世和平。萃諸福以駢臻，合四靈而畢至。肆璇穹錫眷，益隆單厚之釐；乃玉瑞涵姿，正躡明昌之會。産從神后，匪同豹隱於深山；獻自宗藩，迥邁獒來於異域。炳若大人之變，象應河圖；睦然君子之能，名標漢賦。率兹百獸
translation_en:
…restraining its might, it spreads a spirit of kindness and concord; displaying its virtue, it adorns a reign of harmony and prosperity. This divine creature first appeared in Yao’s time: clouds stirred upon the lofty hills, bringing forth primordial essence to assist Shun; cool winds sped along distant roads, drawn by enlightened sageliness to seek allegiance to Tang. When the house of Zhou arose, it entered the poets’ songs. Feeding on blossoms and walking among reeds, it rooted itself in the loyalty and generosity of western Qi; nurtured in purity among gardens and groves, it manifested auspicious blessings in the southern lands. Through the closing ages of the Three Dynasties, scarcely more than its reputation was transmitted; after a thousand years, its form has now appeared again.
We reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor embodies sagely wisdom and possesses divine intelligence, holds fast to the mean and promulgates proper standards. Amid red radiance, your tiger-like transformation reveals the true token of Heaven’s great mandate; from the Purple Pole, your dragon-like ascent accords with the flourishing age of Chonghua, the sage Shun. The myriad states turn within your palm because you extend your compassionate heart; the peoples of the four quarters lie within your gaze as you enlarge your capacity to embrace them. In accordance with the seasons, you abundantly nurture all things and bring the world to peace and harmony. Every blessing gathers and arrives together; all four numinous creatures assemble and appear. Thus the jeweled heavens bestow their favor, increasingly magnifying their abundant blessings; and this jade-like auspicious creature reveals its form precisely at this moment of enlightened prosperity. Born in Shenhou [?], it is unlike a leopard hidden deep in the mountains; presented by a prince of the imperial clan, it far surpasses the mastiff brought from a foreign land. Resplendent like the transformation of a great man, its markings correspond to the River Chart; harmonious in the capacity of a gentleman [?], its name stands celebrated in Han rhapsodies. Leading these hundred beasts…

懽宇宙清寧慶歸馬放牛之候風雲際遇

punctuated:
般般舞虞帝之廷，羣彼五豵，濯濯擾文王之囿，傍翠華而翊聖，依丹闕以懷仁。麟時偕遊，聿著太平之治；鵲巢妙應，永觀王道之成。是宜薦郊廟以升馨，勒鼎彛而傳美者也。
臣等才本駑乘，愧馳驅而莫効；官聯鵷序，倍翔舞以均懽。宇宙清寧，慶歸馬放牛之候；風雲際遇，効攀龍附鳳之忱。仰昊貺之無倫，瞻天顏之有喜，濡毫作頌，稽首颺言。伏願駿業彌昌，鰲圖孔固，跂行喙息，舉安性命之情；岳貢川珍，盡發乾坤之祕。書同文，車同軌，大一統之皇輿；地與久，天與長，介萬年之聖壽。臣等無任瞻
translation_en:
…with patterned coats, they dance in the court of the Emperor of Yu; grouped with those five young boars, sleek and glossy, they dwell tamely in King Wen’s park. Beside the kingfisher-feathered imperial standard, they attend the Sage; near the vermilion palace gates, they cherish benevolence. The qilin roams with them in season [?], thus manifesting the government of Great Peace; the wondrous fulfillment of “The Magpie’s Nest” reveals for all time the accomplishment of the Kingly Way. This indeed deserves to be presented at the suburban sacrifices and in the ancestral temple, its fragrance ascending, and to be inscribed on bronze tripods and ritual vessels so that its glory may be transmitted.
We, your servants, have talents no better than those of inferior carriage horses, and are ashamed that our exertions have brought no result. Joining the ordered ranks of officials, we redouble our jubilant dancing to share in the joy. With the universe tranquil, we celebrate an age when warhorses are returned and oxen set free; favored with this meeting of wind and cloud, we offer the devotion of those who cling to the dragon and attach themselves to the phoenix. Looking up to Heaven’s incomparable bounty and beholding joy upon Your Majesty’s countenance, we wet our brushes to compose this eulogy, bow our heads to the ground, and raise our voices.
We humbly wish that your great enterprise may flourish ever more and that your realm, founded upon the giant turtle, may stand utterly firm; that all creatures that crawl or breathe may find security in their natural lives; and that the tribute of the mountains and treasures of the rivers may fully disclose the hidden riches of Heaven and Earth. May writing share one script and carriages one gauge, bringing grand unity to the imperial domain; may your sagely life endure as long as Earth and Heaven, blessed for ten thousand years. We, your servants, cannot restrain ourselves as we gaze upward…

translation_en:
…gazing toward Heaven and looking up in reverence to Your Majesty, we rejoice and leap for joy in the utmost degree. We respectfully submit this memorial of congratulations for Your Majesty’s hearing.
Third Session
Five Policy Questions
First Question
Cheng Zhongyin
Associate Examiner Luo, Secretary, comments: “The virtue and achievements of our two founders and His Majesty equal Heaven. Even officials of literary learning, long steeped in their beneficence, cannot easily describe them. This composition alone succeeds in proclaiming them. I privately hold out hopes that you will become an official of commanding literary talent.”
Associate Examiner Zhang, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “The virtue and achievements of our two founders far surpass those of antiquity. His Majesty carries forward their excellence and matches their glory: all this is rooted in the transmission of the learning of the mind. The praises of Confucian officials have not expressed even one ten-thousandth of it. Yet you aspire to set forth this abundant glory in full, looking to officials of commanding literary talent to do so. Surely you have long harbored sincere loyalty and sought to put yourself at the service of the throne?”

text:

翔洽已久而欲歌誦其盛者宜錄以
獻
帝王建鴻德於上則鴻烈茂著是故其功
業也必彌綸乎宇宙焉其治化也必超越
乎古今焉而為之臣者不能秉鴻筆以紀

神聖之君而不能摛詞掞藻敷德演功以歌詠
太平之實雍容明盛之休顧不恥歟請因
明問而敬陳之夫有一代之興必有一代
首出之君紹天闡繹以開懿鑠之治有一
代之君亦必有一代博雅之臣揚休述美
以宣純曜之光自昔德業之鴻莫過於唐
punctuated:
皇上天縱聖神，功業振古，蕩乎無能名焉！吾子有望於鴻筆之文，盖翔洽已久，而欲歌誦其盛者，宜錄以獻。

帝王建鴻德於上，則鴻烈茂著。是故其功業也，必彌綸乎宇宙焉；其治化也，必超越乎古今焉。而為之臣者，不能秉鴻筆以紀之，則功業之隆，輝映當年爾矣，而未必聞萬世也；治化之盛，橫被無外爾矣，而未必流無疆也。司馬遷曰：「主上明聖，而德不布聞，有司之過也。」王通亦曰：「有美不揚，天下何觀？」通經綴文之士，際昌隆之世，遇神聖之君，而不能摛詞掞藻，敷德演功，以歌詠太平之實，雍容明盛之休，顧不耻歟？請因明問而敢陳之。夫有一代之興，必有一代首出之君，紹天闡繹，以開懿鑠之治；有一代之君，亦必有一代博雅之臣，揚休述美，以宣純曜之光。自昔德業之鴻，莫過於唐
translation_en:
… His Majesty is endowed by Heaven with sageliness and spiritual insight; his achievements surpass all antiquity, so vast that words cannot name them! You show promise in writing of grand scope. Such flourishing has long prevailed [?], and a composition seeking to celebrate its fullness in song and praise deserves to be copied out and presented to the throne.

When an emperor establishes great virtue above, magnificent accomplishments become abundantly manifest. Thus his achievements must encompass the universe, and his transforming governance must surpass past and present alike. Yet if those who serve him cannot wield a mighty pen to record them, the grandeur of his achievements will illuminate only his own age and may not become known to ten thousand generations. The fullness of his transforming governance will extend everywhere, leaving nothing beyond its reach, yet may not endure without limit. Sima Qian said: “If the sovereign is enlightened and sage, yet his virtue is not widely made known, the fault lies with the responsible officials.” Wang Tong likewise said: “If excellence is not proclaimed, what will all under Heaven have to look upon?” Should scholars versed in the classics and skilled in composition, living in an age of flourishing prosperity and encountering a spiritually gifted and sage ruler, fail to unfold their language and display their literary brilliance, expound his virtue and amplify his achievements, singing of the realities of great peace and celebrating with dignity the blessings of enlightened prosperity—would this not be shameful? Allow me, in response to your discerning question, to venture an account.

Whenever a dynasty rises, there must be a ruler preeminent in his age who carries forward Heaven’s purpose and unfolds it, inaugurating splendid governance. Wherever there is such a dynastic ruler, there must also be learned and cultivated ministers of that age who proclaim his blessings and recount his excellence, spreading the light of his pure radiance. Since antiquity, none has surpassed in grandeur of virtue and achievement Tang …

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
虞三代而當時之臣所稱列而褒載者見
於詩書可攷矣若益之賛堯夔之歌舜禹
湯之績陳於謨誥文武之芳播於雅頌是
時上有鴻德之君而其臣皆能表之下有
鴻筆之臣而其君足以當之灝灝乎渢渢
乎莫得而尚已裔是而降在漢則司馬相
如侈主德之豐廣取徵於神異班固遡炎
祚之融朗系統於帝堯在唐則張說獻握
符之頌揚厲治功柳宗元譔貞符之篇昭
===
顯瑞應至邵雍則以五事論宋治焉曰受
命之日市不易肆曰克服天下在即位之
後曰未嘗殺一無罪曰百年方四葉曰百
年無腹心患是數臣者崇論竑議載國德
於傳書之上宣榮名於萬世之後庶幾鴻
筆之臣矣而當時之君或不足於鴻德政
治小康而心學靡究安能上窺帝王之閫
奧而下副諸臣之紀頌耶洪惟我
太祖高皇帝誕膺

punctuated: 虞三代，而當時之臣所稱列而褒載者，見於《詩》《書》可攷矣。若益之賛堯，夔之歌舜，禹湯之績陳於謨誥，文武之芳播於雅頌，是時上有鴻德之君，而其臣皆能表之；下有鴻筆之臣，而其君足以當之。灝灝乎！渢渢乎！莫得而尚已。裔是而降，在漢則司馬相如侈主德之豐，廣取徵於神異；班固遡炎祚之融，朗系統於帝堯。在唐則張說獻《握符》之頌，揚厲治功；柳宗元譔《貞符》之篇，昭顯瑞應。至邵雍，則以五事論宋治焉：曰受命之日，市不易肆；曰克服天下，在即位之後；曰未嘗殺一無罪；曰百年方四葉；曰百年無腹心患。是數臣者，崇論竑議，載國德於傳書之上，宣榮名於萬世之後，庶幾鴻筆之臣矣。而當時之君，或不足於鴻德，政治小康，而心學靡究，安能上窺帝王之閫奧，而下副諸臣之紀頌耶？洪惟我太祖高皇帝誕膺
translation_en:
…Yu and the Three Dynasties; what their ministers celebrated and recorded in praise can be examined in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents. Thus Yi praised Yao, and Kui sang of Shun; the achievements of Yu and Tang were set forth in the Counsels and Announcements, and the glorious virtues of Wen and Wu were spread through the Elegantiae and Eulogies. In those times, above were rulers of magnificent virtue whose ministers could all give it expression; below were ministers of magnificent literary talent whose rulers were worthy of their praise. How vast! How richly harmonious! Nothing could surpass them.

In subsequent ages, under the Han, Sima Xiangru elaborated upon the abundance of his sovereign’s virtue, drawing widely upon supernatural marvels as evidence. Ban Gu traced the flourishing imperial fortunes of the Han, associated with fire, and clearly linked its succession to Emperor Yao. Under the Tang, Zhang Yue presented his eulogy Holding the Tally (Wo fu), extolling the achievements of government; Liu Zongyuan composed his essay The True Tally (Zhen fu), making auspicious responses manifest. Later, Shao Yong discussed the government of the Song in terms of five matters: on the day its founder received the Mandate, the markets continued undisturbed; he conquered and subdued the realm after ascending the throne; he never killed a single innocent person; a hundred years encompassed only four generations; and for a hundred years there was no danger at the heart of the state.

These ministers, with their lofty arguments and expansive discussions, recorded the dynasty’s virtues in writings handed down to posterity and proclaimed its glorious name to countless later generations. They came close to being ministers of magnificent literary talent. Yet the rulers of their times sometimes fell short in magnificent virtue: their government achieved a modest degree of order, but they did not thoroughly investigate the learning of the mind. How could they attain the innermost mysteries of the ancient emperors and kings above, and measure up to their ministers’ records and eulogies below?

We reverently reflect that our Taizu, the Gao Emperor, grandly received…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
寶命再開渾淪軼駕三五垂統億萬巍巍赫赫
盛矣有竊窺弘猷彙以五事者曰攘克夷
狄以收復中夏也曰肇基南服而統一天
下也曰威加勝國而鋒刄不交也曰躬自
創造而臨御最久也曰申明
祖訓而家法最嚴也非近時詞臣謝鐸之言乎
有鋪敘景炎賛以六事者曰功高萬古也
曰得國之正也曰獨禀全智也曰敬天勤
民也曰家法之嚴也曰兵刑有統也非
===
國初儒臣宋濂之序乎鐸也紀盛於累洽之
餘故述其貽謀者遠濂也對揚於親炙之
日故侈其締業者隆執事所謂舉閎鉅者
言之非耶至於制禮作樂立綱陳紀經野
體國設官分職揆文奮武備邊養民規模
之宏遠節目之周悉則窮年不能闡其妙
罄竹不能殫其書矣逮我
成祖文皇帝光承洪緒密運神機奠鼎幽燕耀
威朔漠肆丕基之耆定乃文教之崇興表

translation_en:
…the precious Mandate, reopening the primordial cosmos, surpassing the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, and establishing a succession for countless generations: how lofty, how glorious, how magnificent! One writer, venturing to discern his grand designs, grouped them under five achievements: driving out and overcoming the barbarians to recover the Central Lands; laying his foundations in the southern regions and unifying All-under-Heaven; overawing the preceding dynasty without blades clashing; personally founding the dynasty and reigning for an exceptionally long time; and promulgating the Ancestral Injunctions, making the rules of the imperial house exceptionally strict. Are these not the words of the recent court literary official Xie Duo? Another writer set forth his resplendent glory, praising him under six headings: achievements surpassing all antiquity; the righteousness of his acquisition of the realm; his unique possession of comprehensive wisdom; his reverence for Heaven and diligent care for the people; the strictness of his house rules; and the orderly control of military affairs and punishments. Is this not the preface by Song Lian, the scholarly official of the dynasty’s founding years? Xie Duo recorded this flourishing greatness after successive ages of peaceful rule, and therefore described the far-reaching plans bequeathed to posterity. Song Lian extolled the emperor while personally receiving his instruction, and therefore magnified the grandeur of his founding achievement. Is this not what you, honored examiners, mean by selecting the greatest matters for discussion? As for instituting rites and creating music, establishing guiding principles and setting out regulations, ordering the countryside and planning the capital, creating offices and assigning duties, directing civil affairs and displaying martial strength, defending the frontiers and nourishing the people—the vast reach of these arrangements and the exhaustive care of their details are such that a lifetime could not elucidate their subtleties, nor could all the bamboo available for writing exhaust the account of them.

He established his capital in Youyan and displayed his might in the northern deserts. translation_en:
…set forth the Way of the sages in the Six Classics and established rules and institutions in the Instructions for the Inner Quarters. In thus fostering the virtue inherited through the generations and perpetuating the dynasty’s flourishing fortune, he truly matched Taizu. At that time his servants praised him, saying: “His magnificent accomplishments and mighty achievements stand preeminent among all kings.” How true those words were!

Our present Emperor, endowed with the qualities of the highest sage, presides over an age of restoration. He reveres Heaven and models himself on his ancestors, upholds the enduring norms and orders human relationships. His consummate virtue communicates with the spirits, and his grand achievements extend over the whole realm. Everything he has established surpasses even remotest antiquity and is rarely seen. Even if Ma and Ban took up their writing brushes, and Zhang and Liu moistened theirs, how could they describe so much as one ten-thousandth of it? Nevertheless, I have heard a little of the grandeur of his accomplishments.

For example, he established the system of separate sacrifices in the four suburban precincts, through which sincerity and reverence silently secure a response. He enhanced the rites of the Great Sacrifice in the Hall of Light, fully fulfilling both reverence for his father as a sovereign and affection for him as a parent. Keeping his parents in mind with filial devotion, he undertook a great imperial progress on his southern tour. His Way accords with the longing that sees a departed parent in one’s soup and against the wall; he solemnized exalted sacrifices in the eastern chamber. Building the Imperial Historical Repository honored the recorded ancestral instructions; commissioning the Zhuixian Pavilion took ancestral virtue as a model. He opened a residence in the imperial park to emphasize the work of farming and sericulture, and removed the Mongol Yuan rulers from sacrificial worship to safeguard the distinction between the non-Chinese and the Chinese. Every itemized memorial submitted by his ministers receives an immediate decision; every classified report from the regions receives his personal scrutiny. August Heaven has manifestly responded, and yet…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
聖誠愈篤也故祈報必順其時黎庶底寧矣而
宸衷愈切也故守令必慎其選盖無一念不體
乎天意無一時不軫乎民生仁恩周浹道
化旁通充滿兩間苞裹六極祥符之協應
治化之雍熈不有以覲揚
二祖之光烈哉今夫五緯耀芒萬古不晦得所
麗也百川分流萬古不息得所歸也窺閎
鉅之休而究精微之極原原本本要有自
矣是故觀心有亭無逸有論釋洪範庶徵
===
之訓書大學衍義之文此
太祖格心之學也謂堯舜相傳惟在允執厥中
謂心能靜虛自然純是天理文華寶鑑之
輯聖學心法之書此
成祖端本之學也我
皇上敬一有箴五箴有註于以直内而存誠重
華有詠翊學有詩于以養心而窮理精一
之旨遠有所承本原之探近有所紹是

聖誠愈篤也，故祈報必順其時；黎庶底寧矣，而宸衷愈切也，故守令必慎其選。盖無一念不體乎天意，無一時不軫乎民生。仁恩周浹，道化旁通，充滿兩間，苞裹六極。祥符之協應，治化之雍熈，不有以覲揚二祖之光烈哉？
今夫五緯耀芒，萬古不晦，得所麗也；百川分流，萬古不息，得所歸也。窺閎鉅之休，而究精微之極，原原本本，要有自矣。是故觀心有亭，無逸有論，釋《洪範》庶徵之訓，書《大學衍義》之文，此太祖格心之學也。謂堯舜相傳，惟在允執厥中；謂心能靜虛，自然純是天理。《文華寶鑑》之輯，《聖學心法》之書，此成祖端本之學也。我皇上《敬一》有箴，《五箴》有註，于以直内而存誠；《重華》有詠，《翊學》有詩，于以養心而窮理。精一之旨，遠有所承；本原之探，近有所紹。是二祖作於先，而弘創制立法之規，
translation_en:
…His Majesty’s sincerity grows ever more profound, and thus prayers and thanksgiving are always offered at their proper seasons. The common people have attained peace, yet his imperial concern grows ever more earnest, and thus prefects and magistrates are invariably selected with care. Indeed, not a single thought fails to embody Heaven’s intent, nor does a single moment pass without concern for the people’s livelihood. His benevolence and grace reach everywhere; his transforming moral influence extends in all directions, filling the space between Heaven and Earth and encompassing the six extremities. Do not the answering auspicious signs and the harmony of his transforming governance serve to manifest and exalt the glorious achievements of the two ancestral emperors?
Now, the five planets shine, their radiance undimmed through all ages, because they have their proper places of attachment; the hundred rivers flow in separate courses, never ceasing through all ages, because they have their proper destinations. When we survey the grandeur of these blessings and investigate their subtlest reaches, tracing their origins to their roots, they must ultimately have a source. Thus there was a pavilion for contemplating the mind and a discourse on freedom from idleness; there were explanations of the teachings on the various signs in the Great Plan and transcriptions of passages from the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning. This was Taizu’s learning of rectifying the mind. It was said that what Yao and Shun transmitted to one another lay solely in sincerely holding fast to the mean, and that if the mind could be still and empty, it would naturally consist purely of Heaven’s principle. The compilation of the Precious Mirror of Literary Splendor and the writing of the Methods of the Mind in Sagely Learning exemplified Chengzu’s learning of setting the root aright. Our emperor has composed an admonition on Reverent Unity and annotations to the Five Admonitions, thereby making his inner life upright and preserving sincerity. He has composed verses on Chonghua—the redoubled splendor associated with Shun—and poems on Assisting Learning, thereby nurturing the mind and investigating principle to its utmost. The purport of refinement and single-mindedness has been inherited from the distant past; the investigation of the fundamental source continues a more recent legacy. Thus the two ancestral emperors arose first and enlarged the framework for creating institutions and establishing laws…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
皇上繼於後而致垂拱平成之化有由然矣槩
而觀之
三聖鴻德之隆奚啻比隆唐虞三代巳耶顧鴻
筆俊儒莫之有作而鴻文瓌藻未見於時
至使簡編之錄闕而不備歌頌之聲鬱而
不宣遐方殊俗靡所睹記得非儒臣學士
之責乎意者天地之廣大縱橫難數滄海
之極深揭厲難測耶夫追典紹謨歸雅還
頌益夔諸賢固未易跂及也至紬繹忠愛
===
之思連結弘麗之篇以彪炳
上德恢張國竒如漢唐諸臣其弗可媲匹之乎
絃歌爲妙異之曲坐者稱善詞臣揚
聖國妙異之政天下有不聳觀其殊卓萬口有
不膾炙其浩爛者耶不然長古而短今渥
前而薄後厥咎將誰任也愚生慨於中乆
矣敢以是而復明問
第二問
黃洪憲

punctuated:
皇上繼於後，而致垂拱平成之化，有由然矣。槩而觀之，三聖鴻德之隆，奚啻比隆唐虞三代巳耶？顧鴻筆俊儒莫之有作，而鴻文瓌藻未見於時，至使簡編之錄闕而不備，歌頌之聲鬱而不宣，遐方殊俗靡所睹記，得非儒臣學士之責乎？意者天地之廣大，縱橫難數；滄海之極深，揭厲難測耶？夫追典紹謨，歸雅還頌，益夔諸賢固未易跂及也。至紬繹忠愛之思，連結弘麗之篇，以彪炳上德，恢張國竒，如漢唐諸臣，其弗可媲匹之乎？絃歌爲妙異之曲，坐者稱善；詞臣揚聖國妙異之政，天下有不聳觀其殊卓，萬口有不膾炙其浩爛者耶？不然，長古而短今，渥前而薄後，厥咎將誰任也？愚生慨於中乆矣，敢以是而復明問。

第二問

黃洪憲
translation_en:
…His Majesty has succeeded them and brought about a transformation in which the world is ordered and at peace while he rules with folded hands: this indeed has its foundation. Viewed as a whole, how could the magnificent virtue of these three sage rulers merely equal that of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties? Yet no accomplished writers or outstanding scholars have undertaken to record it, and no grand compositions or splendid literary works have appeared in our time. Consequently, the written records remain incomplete, voices of praise remain pent up and unheard, and distant lands with differing customs have nothing to consult or record. Is this not the responsibility of scholarly officials and men of learning? Or is it that the vastness of Heaven and Earth defies reckoning in every direction, and the ocean’s utmost depths cannot be fathomed by wading, whether with garments raised or otherwise?

To follow the Canons and continue the Counsels, to return to the Elegantiae and Hymns—such worthies as Yi and Kui are certainly not easily equaled. But as for drawing out thoughts of loyalty and love, composing magnificent and beautiful works to display the sovereign’s virtue and proclaim the wonders of the realm, as did the ministers of the Han and Tang, could we not match them? When singers accompanied by strings perform an exquisite and extraordinary melody, those seated acclaim it. If literary officials extol the exquisite and extraordinary governance of the sage ruler’s realm, would anyone under Heaven fail to gaze in admiration at its singular excellence? Would its vast splendor fail to win praise from every mouth? Otherwise, if we exalt antiquity and belittle the present, lavish praise on earlier times and slight later ones, who will bear the blame? This humble student has long felt indignation in his heart over this, and ventures to offer these words in reply to your discerning question.

Second Question

Huang Hongxian

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
同考試官署郎中吳批考索精詳博而有見非
徒摭拾陳言者佳士佳士
同考試官檢討吳批近時士子類能談說理
道至博物之學漫不究心讀此策足以破其陋
習矣
同考試官編修張批博辨之學聖門不廢要
在有得於道焉爾子能條析往古歸本孔顏殆
知遠覽而有心見者
同考試官修撰丁批博物一策士子類勦浮
===
言殊無足觀茲獨剖析前聞歷如指掌必博雅
士也取之
考試官學士董批博學固難而知要尤難此作
雅醇可想見其人殆知要矣
考試官大學士袁批超識閎覽通人之達觀也然
聖賢之學固自有在子志於博雅而不詭於大道
非天下竒士耶
夫物粲然示人文矣故周物者存乎智夫
道渾然示人精矣故會道者存乎心文者

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
道之寓也精者物之本也文有不周則心
爲有外無以盡散殊之用精有不會則智
爲狥物無以達貫通之原是故物以道觀
智以心運文以精貫用以原該君子所以
究性命之情綜庶類之紀窮幽深之故而
極古今之變也有由矣執事以格物之學
下詢盖欲觀諸生博聞辨智何如也末學
固陋請以謏聞效之可乎夫君子之學求
以致道也而亦貴於博物者何也吾嘗遡
===
觀道始而知物之原矣形氣未分太極既
立二儀肇判萬化斯彰道爲物主而主者
不可測也物由道生而生者不可窮也依
形附氣象聲肖貌翹翾蠕蝝巍偉譎異大
荒絶域昆蟲草木之賾往古來今寒暑日
月之運夏革不能陳其端齊諧不能志其
幻九牧之金不能備其狀隸首之算不能
紀其數夫人處天地之中賦萬形之一自
非精心内照通智外周安能枚舉而縷析

punctuated: 道之寓也，精者物之本也。文有不周，則心爲有外，無以盡散殊之用；精有不會，則智爲狥物，無以達貫通之原。是故物以道觀，智以心運，文以精貫，用以原該，君子所以究性命之情、綜庶類之紀、窮幽深之故而極古今之變也，有由矣。執事以格物之學下詢，盖欲觀諸生博聞辨智何如也。末學固陋，請以謏聞效之，可乎？夫君子之學，求以致道也，而亦貴於博物者，何也？吾嘗遡觀道始，而知物之原矣。形氣未分，太極既立；二儀肇判，萬化斯彰。道爲物主，而主者不可測也；物由道生，而生者不可窮也。依形附氣，象聲肖貌，翹翾蠕蝝，巍偉譎異，大荒絶域，昆蟲草木之賾，往古來今，寒暑日月之運，夏革不能陳其端，齊諧不能志其幻，九牧之金不能備其狀，隸首之算不能紀其數。夫人處天地之中，賦萬形之一，自非精心内照、通智外周，安能枚舉而縷析
translation_en:
…is where the Way lodges; essence is the root of things. If patterned manifestations are not comprehensively understood, the mind leaves something outside its scope and cannot fully comprehend their diverse functions. If essence is not apprehended, knowledge becomes subservient to things and cannot reach the source that unites them all. Thus things are viewed through the Way, knowledge is directed by the mind, patterned manifestations are united through essence, and functions are comprehended through their source. Herein lies the means by which the gentleman investigates the true circumstances of human nature and destiny, gathers together the ordering principles of the many kinds of things, fathoms the causes of what is hidden and profound, and comprehends the full extent of change from antiquity to the present.

You, honored examiners, have deigned to inquire about the learning of investigating things, presumably wishing to see how broad the candidates’ learning is and how discerning their understanding. I, a humble student of limited understanding, beg leave to offer my meager knowledge in response. May I do so? The gentleman’s learning seeks to attain the Way; why, then, does it also prize extensive knowledge of things? I have traced the Way back to its beginning and thereby understood the source of things. Before form and vital energy were differentiated, the Supreme Ultimate was already established; when the Two Modes—Heaven and Earth—first separated, the myriad transformations became manifest. The Way governs things, yet that which governs cannot be fathomed. Things are born from the Way, yet what is born cannot be exhausted.

Things depend upon form and attach to vital energy, manifesting sounds and assuming appearances: creatures that soar and flutter, crawl and wriggle; things towering, magnificent, strange, and extraordinary; the mysteries of insects, plants, and trees in the great wilderness and remote regions; and, throughout past and present, the cycles of cold and heat, sun and moon. Xia Ge could not enumerate their beginnings; Qi Xie could not record their marvels; the metal contributed by the nine regional governors could not fully depict their forms; and Li Shou’s calculations could not reckon their numbers. Now human beings dwell between Heaven and Earth, endowed with but one of the myriad forms. Unless they refine their minds to illuminate what is within and extend their understanding to encompass what is without, how can they enumerate each thing and analyze it thread by thread…

punctuated: 之哉？嘗觀春秋之世，列國之大夫類多閎深辨博，貫淹古今。著《牧民》《山高》《乘馬》《輕重》《九府》之篇，則有若管敬仲焉；讀《三墳》《五典》《八索》《九丘》之書，則有若左史倚相焉。聘晉而識實沈、臺駘之祟，非子產乎？龍見而爲御龍、豢龍之說，非蔡墨乎？夫管子之書，遷史善其詳矣。謹政通商，均役盡利，一匡之業，由此其選也。粹羽純玉，殆有得於聚意者歟？倚相之博，楚國以爲望焉。章華肆侈，申公進規，祈招之詩，由此其誦也。式玉式金，殆善陳夫王度者歟？原參商之構怨，而謂疾非由祟，僑也知鬼神之狀矣；辨董劉之世掌，而謂非龍實智，墨也達人官之能矣。數子者，豈徒以才知之美，而遂能博通若此哉？夷考其時，周典未亡，皇覽具在。伯益之所紀述，外史之所掌達，名山秘藏、金版玉箱之錄，神經怪諜、紫臺丹洞之簡，與夫治國肥家之術、刺世誡俗之言，備矣。賢
translation_en:
…them one by one and analyze them in detail? I have observed that, in the Spring and Autumn period, the grand masters of the various states were generally profound in understanding and broad in discernment, thoroughly versed in antiquity and their own times. Among those who composed such chapters as Governing the People, The Mountain’s Height, Riding Horses, Light and Heavy, and The Nine Treasuries was Guan Jingzhong. Among those who read such works as the Three Tombs, Five Canons, Eight Cords, and Nine Mounds was Yixiang, the Scribe of the Left. Was it not Zichan who, on a diplomatic mission to Jin, recognized the baleful influence of Shichen and Taidai? Was it not Cai Mo who, when a dragon appeared, explained the traditions of the Dragon Drivers and Dragon Rearers?
As for the writings of Master Guan, Sima Qian’s history praises their thoroughness. Attending carefully to government, facilitating commerce, equalizing labor service, and making full use of resources: from these came his outstanding achievement in bringing the realm into order. Fine feathers and pure jade—did he perhaps gain some understanding through concentrating his mind? [?] For his extensive learning, Yixiang was esteemed as an eminent figure in Chu. When extravagance ran unchecked at Zhanghua, the Duke of Shen offered a remonstrance; it was on this occasion that the poem Qizhao was recited. “Like jade, like gold”—was he perhaps skilled in setting forth the standards of a king?
Tracing the origins of the enmity between Shen and Shang, and declaring that the illness did not arise from a spirit’s curse, Qiao [Zichan] understood the nature of ghosts and spirits. Distinguishing the hereditary responsibilities of the Dong and Liu lineages, and saying that it was not the dragons that truly possessed wisdom [?], Mo understood the capacities of human officeholders. Could these men have attained such comprehensive learning merely through their exceptional talent and intelligence?
On examining their times, we find that the canons of Zhou had not yet been lost and that the imperial collections were still intact. The accounts recorded by Bo Yi; the materials kept and transmitted by the Outer Scribe; writings secretly stored in famous mountains, recorded on gold tablets and kept in jade chests; sacred scriptures and records of marvels, and writings from purple terraces and cinnabar grottoes; together with methods for governing states and enriching households, and words criticizing the age and admonishing prevailing customs—all were available. The worthy…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
者學其大不賢者學其小譬之入都多奇
觀入市見異貨總攬而兼蓄之燁然著稱
稱于當時流景曜于後代宜也迨秦火既
燔漢籍未著經生學士專門師授斷編殘
簡猶不得其全而欲冥覽詭奇極命庶物
斯已難矣然亦有若東方朔辨騶牙之瑞
董仲舒達重常之鳥終軍別豹文之鼯鼠
劉向究疏屬之貳負類能察象于耳目之
外定名于疆域之表動色縉紳震悚觀聽
===
一何偉耶夫下帷發憤潜心大業者篤矣
文史三冬萬言足用其自表非誇也條奏
秘書博綜羣籍者至矣幼學能文異材召
見其自負不羣也矧去古伊邇遺文稍稍
復出庸心考覈者無頑鄙之訾深知道術
者無淺閹之毀即春秋諸大夫奚讓哉嗣
是若雷煥察斗牛之氣而知豐城之二劔
楚材辨角端之異而明天道之不殺窺豹
見其一斑嘗鼎齊其寸臠亦有足多者執

文史三冬萬言足用其自表非誇也條奏

見其自負不羣也矧去古伊邇遺文稍稍
復出庸心考覈者無頑鄙之呰深知道術
者無淺闒之毀即春秋諸大夫奚讓哉嗣
是若雷煥察斗牛之氣而知豐城之二劒
楚材辨角端之異而明天道之不殺窺豹
見其一斑嘗鼎齊其寸臠亦有足多者執
punctuated:
者學其大，不賢者學其小。譬之入都多奇觀，入市見異貨，總攬而兼蓄之，燁然著稱稱于當時，流景曜于後代，宜也。迨秦火既燔，漢籍未著，經生學士專門師授，斷編殘簡猶不得其全，而欲冥覽詭奇，極命庶物，斯已難矣。然亦有若東方朔辨騶牙之瑞，董仲舒達重常之鳥，終軍別豹文之鼯鼠，劉向究疏屬之貳負，類能察象于耳目之外，定名于疆域之表，動色縉紳，震悚觀聽，一何偉耶！
夫下帷發憤，潜心大業者篤矣。文史三冬，萬言足用，其自表非誇也。條奏秘書，博綜羣籍者至矣。幼學能文，異材召見，其自負不羣也。矧去古伊邇，遺文稍稍復出，庸心考覈者無頑鄙之訾，深知道術者無淺閹之毀，即春秋諸大夫奚讓哉！嗣是，若雷煥察斗牛之氣而知豐城之二劔，楚材辨角端之異而明天道之不殺，窺豹見其一斑，嘗鼎齊其寸臠，亦有足多者。執
translation_en:
…the worthy study its greater aspects, and the unworthy its lesser ones. It is like entering a capital and encountering many wondrous sights, or entering a market and seeing unusual wares: they surveyed everything and gathered it all into their learning. It was fitting that their reputations should shine brilliantly in their own time and their radiance pass down to later generations. Once the fires of Qin had burned and the writings of Han had yet to appear, classical scholars and men of learning received instruction from teachers within particular schools. They could not even obtain complete copies of broken volumes and fragmentary texts; how much harder, then, to comprehend obscure marvels and identify the full range of things! Yet there were men such as Dongfang Shuo, who identified the auspicious zouya beast; Dong Zhongshu, who understood the bird of Chongchang [?]; Zhong Jun, who distinguished the leopard-patterned flying squirrel; and Liu Xiang, who investigated Erfu at Shushu [?]. All could discern forms beyond what their own eyes and ears had encountered and establish the names of things beyond the realm’s borders. They made officials change countenance and astonished all who saw and heard them. How magnificent!
Those who lowered their curtains, applied themselves resolutely to study, and concentrated on the great undertaking were indeed devoted. Studying literature and history for three winters, and finding ten thousand words sufficient for practical use: this account of his own attainments was no boast. Those who submitted itemized reports on the writings in the imperial collection and comprehensively mastered the multitude of texts attained the utmost. Learning from childhood, becoming accomplished in composition, and being summoned to an imperial audience for exceptional talent: such confidence in his own ability set him apart from the crowd. Moreover, antiquity was still close at hand, and surviving writings were gradually reappearing. Those who applied their minds to investigation escaped the reproach of obtuse ignorance; those who deeply understood the Way and its arts escaped the charge of shallow narrowness [?]. In what respect need they yield even to the great officers of the Spring and Autumn period? Thereafter, men such as Lei Huan observed the emanations in the constellations Dipper and Ox and thereby knew of the two swords at Fengcheng; Chucai discerned the extraordinary nature of the jiaoduan beast and thereby understood Heaven’s Way of sparing life. Seeing a single spot when glimpsing a leopard, or judging a cauldron’s seasoning from a morsel an inch across, they too had much that deserved praise. You …

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
事謂之通朗信矣嗟夫埳蛙不足以語海
局於量也夏蟲不可以語氷篤於時也人
不博覽則不聞古今不見事類不知然否
與埳蛙夏蟲又何擇焉故鄒衍旁通五德
侈談裨海遂使梁惠郊迎燕昭擁篲彼移
監之不知其官貂蟬之不諳其義顧問之
列有餘恶矣博物之學固君子所不廢哉
且古今所稱大聖人者莫孔子若也使博
物而可廢也吾意孔子當存而不論論而
===
不議矣廼今觀之楚江拾果析以萍實季
井得犬繹以羵羊鳥舞齊也推恒雨之徵
隼止陳也闡楛矢之遺而專車之骨又指
為防風氏所遺焉探賾索隱鈎深致遠總
統百家包羅萬代非特漢晉諸人莫能窺
其畔岸即春秋數子亦未足涉其津涯豈
誠資于好問而得于敏求者哉備天地之
美稱神明之容内聖外王六通四辟天下
之道咸該昭曠之原而通睿哲之臨矣是故

之道咸該昭曠之原而通睿哲之臨是故
punctuated: 事謂之通朗，信矣。嗟夫！埳蛙不足以語海，局於量也；夏蟲不可以語氷，篤於時也。人不博覽，則不聞古今，不見事類，不知然否，與埳蛙夏蟲又何擇焉？故鄒衍旁通五德，侈談裨海，遂使梁惠郊迎，燕昭擁篲。彼移監之不知其官，貂蟬之不諳其義，顧問之列有餘恶矣。博物之學，固君子所不廢哉！且古今所稱大聖人者，莫孔子若也。使博物而可廢也，吾意孔子當存而不論，論而不議矣。廼今觀之，楚江拾果，析以萍實；季井得犬，繹以羵羊；鳥舞齊也，推恒雨之徵；隼止陳也，闡楛矢之遺；而專車之骨，又指為防風氏所遺焉。探賾索隱，鈎深致遠，總統百家，包羅萬代，非特漢晉諸人莫能窺其畔岸，即春秋數子亦未足涉其津涯。豈誠資于好問而得于敏求者哉？備天地之美，稱神明之容，内聖外王，六通四辟，天下之道咸該，昭曠之原而通睿哲之臨矣。是故
translation_en: …you call this comprehensive understanding; truly it is so. Alas! One cannot speak of the sea to a frog in a pit, for its scope confines it; one cannot speak of ice to a summer insect, for its season limits it. If people do not read widely, they will know nothing of past and present, perceive no categories of affairs, and be unable to distinguish what is so from what is not. How then do they differ from the frog in a pit or the summer insect? Thus Zou Yan comprehensively understood the Five Powers and discoursed expansively on the subsidiary seas, inducing King Hui of Liang to welcome him in the suburbs and King Zhao of Yan to take up a broom in his honor. Those who do not know the office denoted by “yijian” [?], or understand the significance of sable tails and cicada ornaments, have ample cause for shame among those consulted by the ruler. Broad knowledge of things is certainly a pursuit that the gentleman cannot abandon! Moreover, among those acclaimed as great sages, past and present, none equals Confucius. If broad knowledge of things could be dispensed with, I think Confucius would have preserved such matters without discussing them, or discussed them without passing judgment. Yet consider what we find: when a fruit was picked up in a river in Chu, he identified it as the fruit of duckweed; when a dog was found in the Ji family's well, he explained that it was a fen sheep, an earth spirit. When a bird danced in Qi, he inferred an omen of prolonged rain; when a falcon alighted in Chen, he explained the provenance of the ku-wood arrow. A bone that filled an entire cart he identified as a remnant of Fangfeng. He explored mysteries and sought out what was hidden, plumbed the depths and reached into the distance, comprehended the hundred schools and encompassed ten thousand generations. Not only could the men of the Han and Jin fail even to glimpse the bounds of his knowledge; even those several masters of the Spring and Autumn period could not reach its shores. Could this truly have depended upon a fondness for questioning and been attained through diligent inquiry? Possessing the full beauty of Heaven and Earth, matching the bearing of divine intelligence, inwardly a sage and outwardly a king, penetrating the six directions and opening out on all four sides, he embraced all the ways of the world. From a source of luminous vastness, his sagacious understanding extended over all [?]. Therefore…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
江海絡於地維寶藏富焉非取足於川瀆
也日月麗乎天經萬象呈焉非有待于爝
火也聖人天聰明之盡萬理涵焉非有俟
于問學也所謂大人之胷懷非一才高智
大無所不包者非孔子孰能當之雖然太
宰訝其多能則以不試自解黨人稱其博
學則以執御自居又若不欲以是爲訓者
當時及門之士若子貢之達冉有之藝夫
子每不滿焉其所亟許而樂予之者顏子
===
一人而已夫顏子博文竭力所見卓爾聞
一知十頓悟如賜且遜避以爲不及顧以
如愚稱而不以博辨自見也觀其言曰我
不能博五經又不能博衆事守信一學不
好廣觀無溫故知新之明而有守愚不覽
之闇嗚呼潜心退省入聖室矣造于眇思
極窅冥之深矣黜聰坐忘無待于外矣今
夫託契鴻濛而聆鈞天之樂者不審夫笙
鏞柷敔之聲游精象罔而獲赤水之珠者

一人而已夫顏子博文竭力所見卓爾聞
一知十穎悟如賜且遜避以爲不及顏以
如愚稱而不以博辨自見也觀其言曰我
不能博五經又不能博衆事守信一學不
好廣觀無濫故知新之明而有守愚不覽
之闢嗚呼潛心退省入聖室矣造于聊思
極窅窅之深矣黜聰坐忘無待于外矣今
夫託契鴻濛而聆鈞天之樂者不審夫笙
鏞柷敔之聲游精象罔而獲赤水之珠者
punctuated:
江海絡於地維，寶藏富焉，非取足於川瀆也；日月麗乎天經，萬象呈焉，非有待于爝火也；聖人天聰明之盡，萬理涵焉，非有俟于問學也。所謂大人之胷懷，非一才，高智大，無所不包者，非孔子孰能當之？雖然，太宰訝其多能，則以不試自解；黨人稱其博學，則以執御自居，又若不欲以是爲訓者。當時及門之士，若子貢之達、冉有之藝，夫子每不滿焉。其所亟許而樂予之者，顏子一人而已。
夫顏子博文竭力，所見卓爾，聞一知十，頓悟如賜，且遜避以爲不及，顧以如愚稱，而不以博辨自見也。觀其言曰：「我不能博五經，又不能博衆事，守信一學，不好廣觀，無溫故知新之明，而有守愚不覽之闇。」嗚呼！潜心退省，入聖室矣；造于眇思，極窅冥之深矣；黜聰坐忘，無待于外矣。今夫託契鴻濛而聆鈞天之樂者，不審夫笙鏞柷敔之聲；游精象罔而獲赤水之珠者，
translation_en:
The rivers and seas interlace the earth’s supporting cords, abounding in precious stores; they do not depend on streams and watercourses for their sufficiency. The sun and moon adhere to heaven’s ordered courses, revealing the myriad forms; they have no need of torchlight. The sage possesses the fullness of Heaven-given perceptiveness [?], encompassing the myriad principles; he need not await inquiry and study. The capacious mind of the great man, unrestricted to a single talent, lofty and vast in wisdom [?], embracing everything—who but Confucius could answer to this description? Nevertheless, when the Grand Steward marveled at his many abilities, he explained them by saying that he had not been employed in office. When the people of his district praised his extensive learning, he presented himself merely as a driver of chariots. It was as though he did not wish these accomplishments to serve as his teaching. Among those who studied under him at the time, even Zigong, with his understanding, and Ran You, with his abilities, repeatedly fell short of the Master’s expectations. The one whom he frequently praised and gladly commended was Yan Zi alone.
Yan Zi broadened his learning through cultural study and exerted his strength to the utmost; what he perceived stood towering before him. Hearing one thing, he understood ten. Even Ci—that is, Zigong—with his sudden insight, deferred to him and acknowledged that he could not match him. Yet Yan Zi was praised as seeming foolish, and did not display himself through wide learning and disputation. Consider his words: “I cannot master the Five Classics in their breadth, nor can I acquire wide knowledge of the multitude of affairs. I hold faithfully to a single teaching and do not delight in wide-ranging observation. I lack the illumination of one who reviews the old and understands the new; instead, I have the darkness of one who clings to foolishness and does not look widely.” Ah! By concentrating his mind and reflecting in retirement, he entered the sage’s inner chamber. Reaching into subtle thought, he plumbed the depths of the obscure and mysterious. Casting off perceptiveness and sitting in forgetfulness, he depended on nothing external. Now, one who enters into communion with Hongmeng, the primordial vastness, and hears the music of the central heavens does not attend to the sounds of mouth organs, great bells, wooden percussion boxes, and wooden scrapers. One who lets his spirit roam with Xiangwang, the formless, and obtains the pearl of the Red River …

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
不屑夫瑇瑁玟珉之產顏子何嘗不博也
而特不以博辨稱故夫子謂之曰吾服汝
忘也汝之服於我亦忘也是博約之要授
受之微也謂其才智出春秋漢晉諸子之
下可乎蓋諸子者以智觀物周其粲然之
文顏子者以心求道會其渾然之精孔子
則兼道器貫本末小大精粗無乎不運其
明是故守一方之術拘耳目之近而無弘
暢雅閑之識是面墻之陋也離堅合異汎
===
游廣涉聞見雖殫原本則闕是多岐之惑
也之二者失道均矣學者與其騖于外也
寧狥于內何則空器在廚金銀塗之其中
無物饑人不顧殽膳甘醢土釜所盛入者
嚮之其所取者有在也夫道管于心該于

punctuated: 不屑夫瑇瑁玟珉之產。顏子何嘗不博也？而特不以博辨稱。故夫子謂之曰：「吾服汝忘也，汝之服於我亦忘也。」是博約之要、授受之微也。謂其才智出春秋漢晉諸子之下，可乎？蓋諸子者，以智觀物，周其粲然之文；顏子者，以心求道，會其渾然之精。孔子則兼道器，貫本末，小大精粗，無乎不運其明。是故守一方之術，拘耳目之近，而無弘暢雅閑之識，是面墻之陋也；離堅合異，汎游廣涉，聞見雖殫，原本則闕，是多岐之惑也。之二者失道均矣。學者與其騖于外也，寧狥于內。何則？空器在廚，金銀塗之，其中無物，饑人不顧；殽膳甘醢，土釜所盛，入者嚮之，其所取者有在也。夫道管于心，該于物，辨析既精，大原斯會。所貴乎學者，豈徒在物耶？昔人有言：「心如丸卵，為體內藏；眸子如豆，為身光明。」蓋見道器之樞具于我矣。誠能周其粲然者于目，而會其渾然者
translation_en:
…disdains such products as tortoiseshell and ornamental stones. When was Master Yan ever lacking in breadth of learning? He simply was not renowned for wide learning and disputation. Thus the Master said to him: “I admire your forgetting; you, in submitting to me, likewise forget.” This is the essential relationship between breadth and restraint, the subtlety of teaching and receiving instruction. Can one say that his talent and wisdom ranked below those of the various thinkers of the Spring and Autumn period and the Han and Jin dynasties? Those thinkers used their intellect to observe things and encompass their brilliant patterns; Master Yan used his heart to seek the Way and comprehend its undivided essence. Confucius embraced both the Way and its concrete manifestations, linking root and branches; whether small or great, refined or coarse, nothing lay beyond the exercise of his illumination.

Thus, to cling to the techniques of a single field, confined to what lies immediately before one’s ears and eyes, without broad, penetrating, cultivated, and composed understanding, is the ignorance of facing a wall. To distinguish hardness from other qualities and unite differences, roaming widely and ranging broadly, exhausting what can be heard and seen while neglecting its fundamental source, is the confusion of following too many branching paths. These two equally lose the Way. Rather than pursue what is external, the learner should devote himself to what is within. Why? An empty vessel in the kitchen may be coated with gold and silver, but with nothing inside it, a hungry person pays it no attention. Yet dishes of food and savory meat sauces, served in an earthenware pot, attract those who enter: there is something substantive in what they seek.

The Way is gathered within the heart and encompasses all things. Once distinctions have been precisely analyzed, its great source can be comprehended. Can what we value in learning lie merely in things? Someone of old said: “The heart is like a round egg, stored within the body; the pupils are like beans, providing the body with light.” This shows that the pivot joining the Way and its concrete manifestations is present within oneself. If one can truly encompass their brilliant patterns with one’s eyes and comprehend their undivided essence…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
有見矣
考試官大學士袁批金穀之贏縮關國計之盈
虛此方今急務當事者求其策未得也如子所
條列不確乎可行耶
天下之言財計者非有異謀竒論運輸於
財之外也酌損益之宜調盈虚之術以求
所以裕之而已損益勢也勢有所趨而其
本則先於下盈虚權也權有所御而其事
則先於上知勢之在下也從而酌之則損
===
益之宜審矣知權之在上也從而調之則
盈虚之術當矣勢者乗夫上下而爲之酌
焉者也是故言足財者先足其民權者乗
夫利害而爲之調焉者也是故言足財者
務除其害足民所以足國也除害所以興
利也苟於民不加之意而於害財者復叢
業焉吾恐民益以窮財益以耗其患不獨
在生民而且移之國計矣甚矣財計之敝
於天下也執事慮焉而求所以足國裕民

===

馬者也是故言足財者先足其民權者乘
夫利害而爲之調焉者也是故言足財者

於天下也執事慮焉而求所以足國裕民
punctuated:
有見矣。

考試官大學士袁批：金穀之贏縮，關國計之盈虛，此方今急務，當事者求其策未得也。如子所條列，不確乎可行耶？

天下之言財計者，非有異謀竒論，運輸於財之外也，酌損益之宜，調盈虚之術，以求所以裕之而已。損益，勢也；勢有所趨，而其本則先於下。盈虚，權也；權有所御，而其事則先於上。知勢之在下也，從而酌之，則損益之宜審矣；知權之在上也，從而調之，則盈虚之術當矣。勢者，乗夫上下而爲之酌焉者也，是故言足財者先足其民；權者，乗夫利害而爲之調焉者也，是故言足財者務除其害。足民所以足國也，除害所以興利也。苟於民不加之意，而於害財者復叢業焉，吾恐民益以窮，財益以耗，其患不獨在生民，而且移之國計矣。甚矣，財計之敝於天下也！執事慮焉，而求所以足國裕民
translation_en:
…shows insight indeed.

Comment by Examiner Yuan, Grand Secretary: The surplus or shortage of money and grain bears upon the abundance or depletion of state finances. This is an urgent concern today, yet those responsible have sought a solution without finding one. Are not the measures you have enumerated sound and practicable?

Those who discuss public finance throughout the realm do not possess extraordinary schemes or ingenious theories that operate outside the resources themselves. They merely weigh appropriate reductions and increases, and adjust the means of balancing surpluses and deficits, seeking thereby to ensure abundance. Reductions and increases concern prevailing conditions: these conditions have their tendencies, but their foundations lie first among those below. Surpluses and deficits concern discretionary authority: this authority has what it governs, but its exercise lies first with those above. Once one understands that conditions lie among those below and weighs matters accordingly, the appropriate reductions and increases become clear. Once one understands that authority lies with those above and makes adjustments accordingly, the methods for balancing surpluses and deficits become fitting. Assessing conditions means weighing matters in light of the circumstances of those above and below. Thus, anyone who speaks of making resources sufficient must first ensure that the people have enough. Exercising discretion means making adjustments in light of benefits and harms. Thus, anyone who speaks of making resources sufficient must strive to eliminate what causes harm. Providing sufficiently for the people is the means of providing sufficiently for the state; eliminating harm is the means of promoting benefit. If one pays no heed to the people and allows the things that damage financial resources to accumulate further [?], I fear that the people will become ever poorer and resources ever more depleted. The resulting troubles will not afflict the populace alone, but will also extend to state finances. How grave is the deterioration of public finance throughout the realm! Concerned about this, you seek the means to provide sufficiently for the state and bring prosperity to the people…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
之道經生何足以籌此雖然試言之夫今
之言財者有二曰五穀曰五金五穀民資
之以為朝夕養無能一日廢者而所賴以
轉移為用與穀互相資焉者又莫善於金
二者之為生民利誠至博且重矣其在五
行則金金也穀木也五行未嘗偏勝謂有
所缺者非也而曰金無餘氣者盖以金之
行令在秋而其權主殺天道好生故不令
有餘耳若夫五穀亦或有不足者則有說
===
焉嘗以五行生尅之理推之金氣盛則木
氣衰刑罰甲兵以金用也二者交動則金
勝而傷木是以五穀因之焉然則觀於天
人之際而其故可知矣天之道不令金有
餘而人顧從而貴之木之氣常為金所勝
而又從而賤之甚非所以順天之時興地
之利也昔者禹貢九州定賦以秸粟為重
箕疇八政養民以食貨為先七月之詩皆
言農事之候無逸之訓深明小人之依聖

translation_en:
…the way to achieve this—how could a student of the classics be equal to devising it? Nevertheless, let me attempt to speak of it. Those who discuss wealth today speak of two things: the five grains and the five metals. The people rely on the five grains for their sustenance morning and evening; they cannot dispense with them for a single day. Yet for facilitating exchange and use, in mutual support with grain, nothing surpasses metal. The benefits these two bring to the people’s livelihood are indeed exceedingly extensive and important.

Among the Five Phases, metal belongs to Metal, and grain to Wood. None of the Five Phases inherently predominates; it is wrong to say that any is deficient. As for the saying that Metal has no surplus vital force, this is because Metal holds sway in autumn, and its authority governs killing. Heaven’s Way cherishes life and therefore does not allow Metal a surplus. If the five grains sometimes prove insufficient, there is also an explanation. I have considered this through the principles by which the Five Phases generate and overcome one another: when Metal’s vital force flourishes, Wood’s declines. Punishments and warfare employ Metal. When both are set in motion together, Metal prevails and injures Wood; the five grains consequently suffer. Thus, by examining the relations between Heaven and humanity, one may understand the cause.

Heaven’s Way does not permit Metal a surplus, yet people prize it. Wood’s vital force is constantly overcome by Metal, yet people further devalue it. This is very far from following Heaven’s seasons and developing the benefits of the earth. In antiquity, the Tribute of Yu established tribute for the Nine Provinces, giving weight to grain stalks and grain. Among the eight policies in Jizi’s Great Plan, food and goods came first in nourishing the people. The poem Seventh Month speaks throughout of the seasons for agricultural work. The admonitions in Against Idleness explain fully what the common people depend upon. The sages…

title: 嘉靖四十一年會試錄
text:
人治天下能使菽粟如水火而猶重之也
此晁錯謂明君貴五穀而賤金玉其說信
矣顧今之時則有不然者三尺童子授金
而投之忻然咲而不忍釋天下之愛金類
若此至於五穀乃或視輕焉死生飽餒之
繫不遑恤而顧汲汲焉重金者何也夫固
有所用之也自金之用日益侈而上下之
交征也日益甚粟日以賤而金日以詘其
勢必至於俱困而後已司馬光曰天地生
===
財止有此數不在官則在民此其乘除消
長理與事誠然也而今之時則亦有不然
者征求苛煩十室九罄殫竭民間之所有
而歸之公上謂宜盡在官也然歲一不稔
南北之待哺者輒以饑聞是猶可諉也曰
歲也至於金之所入凶年不損豐年不加
而亦有匱焉太倉內帑之所儲積日出而
不給又一切為救濟之術而取盈於經制
常額之外以求足乎金而卒未嘗足何也
